checks.method: rule-based: citation validity, typed fact binding (values, contributions, signs, probabilities, prediction set), class / column / number checks, no value judgements or causal claims, lexical overlap with cited passages, real ATT&CK IDs present in cited passages. Not a semantic proof.

group_xai.detail: 172 flows of 4 attack types explained for the group findings

coverage.selection_rule: Illustrative flows: for each of the four most frequent predicted attack types, the flow at the MEDIAN confidence of that type (a typical case, not the best one); the first flow of the review order (highest heuristic severity, then confidence); and the lowest-confidence flow whose shortlist contains Normal and an attack type (or, if there is none, the lowest-confidence attack-type-uncertain flow). Each card explains one flow, not its whole group.

summary.scope: Offline analysis of 300 completed network flows uploaded as "test_flows.csv". The file contains flow measurements only: no live traffic, IP addresses, ports, timestamps or payloads.

status_confidence.meaning: how sure the model is that a flow is an attack (any type) or Normal: the calibrated probabilities of the nine attack classes added together. The class confidence (above) is about the exact type.

triage_priority.rule: serious flows >= 25% of all flows, or malicious flows >= 50%
triage_priority.meaning: Batch triage priority: an application heuristic that orders review work from the predicted classes and fixed severity rules. It is not a model output, not observed business impact and not a confirmed compromise.

summary.next_check: Find flow #284 (unas/-, state INT, 200 bytes sent, 0 received) in packet captures or sensor logs from the same period and decide whether it is DoS activity.

notes: Probabilities are calibrated on held-out rows of the training file (temperature scaling). They describe the model, not proof, and can be less reliable on traffic that differs from the training data.
The 90% prediction set (shortlist) targets 90% coverage on average over flows like the calibration rows; it is not a per-flow guarantee, and a single-class set is not certainty.

Attack-STATUS uncertain: the shortlist contains Normal and at least one attack type (attack or not is unclear). Attack-TYPE uncertain: predicted attack and the shortlist has several attack types but not Normal.
Confidence, heuristic severity and business impact are different quantities.
shift_evidence: On the official test file (shifted from the training file) the detector flagged 27.2% of Normal flows as attacks (model card).
For the previous detector v2 the 90% sets contained the true class for 79.1% of official test flows (Notebook 21); this was not re-measured for v3.

xai.how_to_read: Each contribution moves the model score of the predicted class up (supports) or down (opposes). Base value + all contributions = the model score; the deployed detector divides it by the temperature and adds a fixed class offset before turning scores into probabilities. Contributions are not percentages of the probability, and they describe the model, not the cause of the traffic.

findings.text: The detector classifies this flow as DoS with calibrated probability 0.58.
The 90% prediction set contains Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, Reconnaissance, so the exact attack type is uncertain.
The value smean = 100 pushed the prediction towards DoS (contribution +1.395).
The value sbytes = 200 pushed the prediction towards DoS (contribution +0.662).
The value proto = unas pushed the prediction towards DoS (contribution +0.343).

explanation.text: The model is 0.58 confident that this flow is DoS with a probability of 0.99 that it is an attack of any type; its 90% prediction set contains Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, and Reconnaissance.
The strongest evidence is smean = 100 (contribution +1.395) and sbytes = 200 (contribution +0.662), while ct_srv_src = 11 argues against DoS (contribution -0.336).
The value smean = 100 occurs in 59 to 130 in the middle half of training Normal flows.
Compared with Exploits, the second most likely class (15.9%), column smean = 100 favours DoS by +0.467 in model score.
In the analysed dataset, 70 flows (26.3% of the predicted attacks) were classified as DoS, with average confidence 0.56.

xai.how_to_read: Each contribution moves the model score of the predicted class up (supports) or down (opposes). Contributions are not percentages of the probability, and they describe the model, not the cause of the traffic.

Network DoS can be performed by exhausting the network bandwidth services rely on. Example resources include specific websites, email services, DNS, and web-based applications. Adversaries have been observed conducting network DoS attacks for political purposes and to support other malicious activities, including distraction, hacktivism, and extortion. A Network DoS will occur when the bandwidth capacity of the network connection to a system is exhausted due to the volume of malicious traffic directed at the resource or the network connections and network devices the resource relies on. For example, an adversary may send 10Gbps of traffic to a server that is hosted by a network with a 1Gbps connection to the internet. This traffic can be generated by a single system or multiple systems spread across the internet, which is commonly referred to as a distributed DoS (DDoS). To perform Network DoS attacks several aspects apply to multiple methods, including IP address spoofing, and botnets. Adversaries may use the original IP address of an attacking system, or spoof the source IP address to make the attack traffic more difficult to trace back to the attacking system or to enable reflection. register.text: Filter Network Traffic: When flood volumes exceed the capacity of the network connection being targeted, it is typically necessary to intercept the incoming traffic upstream to filter out the attack traffic from the legitimate traffic. Such defenses can be provided by the hosting Internet Service Provider (ISP) or by a 3rd party such as a Content Delivery Network (CDN) or providers specializing in DoS mitigations. Depending on flood volume, on-premises filtering may be possible by blocking source addresses sourcing the attack, blocking ports that are being targeted, or blocking protocols being used for transport. As immediate response may require rapid engagement of 3rd parties, analyze the risk associated to critical resources being affected by Network DoS attacks and create a disaster recovery plan/business continuity plan to respond to incidents.

register.text: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application. Tactics: initial-access. Adversaries may attempt to exploit a weakness in an Internet-facing host or system to initially access a network. The weakness in the system can be a software bug, a temporary glitch, or a misconfiguration. Exploited applications are often websites/web servers, but can also include databases (like SQL), standard services (like SMB or SSH), network device administration and management protocols (like SNMP and Smart Install), and any other system with Internet-accessible open sockets. On ESXi infrastructure, adversaries may exploit exposed OpenSLP services; they may alternatively exploit exposed VMware vCenter servers. Depending on the flaw being exploited, this may also involve [Exploitation for Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1211) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203). If an application is hosted on cloud-based infrastructure and/or is containerized, then exploiting it may lead to compromise of the underlying instance or container. This can allow an adversary a path to access the cloud or container APIs (e.g., via the [Cloud Instance Metadata API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005)), exploit container host access via [Escape to Host](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611), or take advantage of weak identity and access management policies. Adversaries may also exploit edge network infrastructure and related appliances, specifically targeting devices that do not support robust host-based defenses. Fo Detection:

bullets.text: 266 of 300 flows (88.7%) were predicted as attacks and 34 as Normal. The largest predicted groups are DoS (70), Exploits (45) and Generic (30).
For the 70 DoS predictions, the most frequent reason was the average packet size sent by the source (a top-three reason in 62 of 70 flows).
For the 45 Exploits predictions, the most frequent reason was the number of recent connections to the same service and destination (a top-three reason in 37 of 45 flows).

For 263 of 300 flows the model is at least 90% sure whether it is an attack; the uncertainty is mostly about the exact type (151 predictions have type confidence below 70%). For 7 flows, Normal traffic is still a possible answer.
These are predictions about completed flows, not confirmed incidents or a forecast of future attacks. Check the flagged flows against logs before blocking anything.

actions.what: Restore and monitor after a confirmed incident
actions.how: See NIST SP 800-184: Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery for additional guidance.
actions.when: Only after a confirmed incident has been contained.
actions.check: Restored systems behave normally and monitoring shows no recurrence for an agreed period.
actions.owner: Incident response lead with the system owners

outcome.evidence_needed: Packet captures, firewall or sensor logs and host logs from the period when the flows were recorded. The uploaded file has no addresses, ports or timestamps, so flows must be matched by protocol, service, state and byte counts.
outcome.confirms: Another source (logs or captures) shows the same activity, for example the same service, volumes and connection pattern as the flagged flows.
weakens: the flagged traffic belongs to a known service, backup, monitoring or test run by your own team
other sensors or logs from the same period show nothing unusual
Normal is still on the shortlist (7 flows)
outcome.mitigation_success: After a confirmed problem is fixed, the activity no longer appears in new captures or logs, and normal services still work.

limits: Predictions are not confirmed incidents; class-to-ATT&CK mappings are hypotheses for context.
No IP addresses, ports, host names, timestamps or payloads are in the uploaded file, so hosts, timelines and botnet or DNS attribution cannot be established.
Detailed explanations cover 6 example flows of 300; other flows of the same type may differ.
